result.markdown: --- title: "Binomial (n = 5, p = 0.1)" subtitle: "Discrete counts of a rare event: highly skewed and lumpy" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Show the simulation code"} source("../R/clt_functions.R") rgen <- function(n) rbinom(n, size = 5, prob = 0.1) # n counts, each 0..5 mu <- 5 * 0.1 # 0.5 sigma <- sqrt(5 * 0.1 * 0.9) # 0.671 pop_skew <- (1 - 2 * 0.1) / sigma # 1.19 pop_kurt <- (1 - 6 * 0.1 * 0.9) / (5 * 0.1 * 0.9) # 1.02 coarse <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 75, 100, 125, 150, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000, 1250, 1500, 2000) exper <- run_with_refinement(rgen, coarse, mu, sigma) res <- exper$results n_main <- smallest_normal_n(res) n_std <- n_by_standard(res) at <- function(k) res[res$n == k, ] save_results(res, "binomial") save_summary(res, "Binomial(5, 0.1)", n_main, prediction = "100", key_note = "Skewness passes early; discreteness (Q-Q steps, jumping tails) sets n") # the exponential results, for comparison in section 7 exp_row <- subset(read.csv("../results/summary.csv"), population == "Exponential(1)") ``` ::: ::: {.answer-box} n = 83 under my main standard (strict standard: ≈ 900 · lenient standard: ≈ 20 · my prediction: 100) ::: ## 1. What population am I sampling from? Each observation counts the successes in 5 tries when each try succeeds with probability 0.1. Think of the number of defective items in a box of five, or the number of goals a player scores in five shots. Most of the time the answer is **0**, sometimes 1, and rarely more. | Property | Value | |---|---| | Possible values | 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 | | Mean μ | np = 0.5 | | Standard deviation σ | √(np(1−p)) ≈ 0.671 | | Skewness | (1−2p)/σ ≈ 1.19 (right skew) | | Excess kurtosis | ≈ 1.02 | | Theoretical SE of the mean | 0.671/√n | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} style_par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)) pmf <- dbinom(0:5, size = 5, prob = 0.1) b <- barplot(pmf, names.arg = 0:5, col = adjustcolor(pal$bars, 0.75), border = NA, ylim = c(0, 0.7), xlab = "Number of successes in 5 tries", ylab = "Probability") text(b, pmf + 0.04, pct(pmf), cex = 0.85, col = pal$ink) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The population: P(0) = 59%, P(1) = 33%, P(2) = 7%, and 3 or more is under 1%.](04_binomial_files/figure-html/fig-population-1.png){#fig-population width=990} ::: ::: ## 2. What did I expect before running the simulation? > **n = 100.** The binomial is less skewed than the exponential, but its values are discrete: the sample > mean can only move in steps of 1/n. In my pilot run the histogram still looked lumpy at n = 20, so I > expected it to need more observations than the exponential before its graph looks smooth and normal. ## 3. Which sample sizes did I investigate? 1. **Coarse grid:** n = 1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 75, 100, 125, 150, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000, 1250, 1500, 2000. It reaches 2,000 to check whether the strict standard stays satisfied beyond 1,000. 2. **Refinement:** every n from 76 to 99. B = 100,000 sample means per n, seed 9426. ## 4. Results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_convergence(res, chosen_n = n_main, theory_skew = pop_skew, theory_kurt = pop_kurt) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The four checks. Skewness (with theory 1.19/√n in orange) passes early; the Q-Q correlation and the tails take much longer.](04_binomial_files/figure-html/fig-convergence-1.png){#fig-convergence width=990} ::: ::: The order in which the checks pass is the key result for this population: | Check | Passes (and stays passed) from | |---|---| | Excess kurtosis | n = 2 | | Skewness | n = 30 (theory: (1.19/0.25)² ≈ 23) | | Q-Q correlation | n = 75 | | Tails | n = 83 | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_show <- c(1, 5, 20, 30, n_main, 300) plot_hist_grid(exper, n_show, mu, sigma, step = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sampling distribution of the mean (one bar per possible value, spaced 1/n apart) and the CLT normal curve.](04_binomial_files/figure-html/fig-hist-1.png){#fig-hist width=990} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_qq_grid(exper, n_show) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Q-Q plots. The points form a staircase because the mean can only take values 1/n apart.](04_binomial_files/figure-html/fig-qq-1.png){#fig-qq width=990} ::: ::: ### Why the tail check jumps around ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} near <- res[res$n >= 40 & res$n <= 150, ] style_par(mar = c(4, 4.4, 1, 1)) plot(near$n, 100 * near$upper_tail, type = "b", pch = 24, col = pal$curve, bg = pal$curve, ylim = range(c(100 * near$lower_tail, 100 * near$upper_tail, 1.75, 3.25)), xlab = "n", ylab = "% of means beyond 1.96 SE") lines(near$n, 100 * near$lower_tail, type = "b", pch = 25, col = pal$bars, bg = pal$bars) rect(0, 1.75, 1e4, 3.25, col = adjustcolor(pal$zone, 0.10), border = NA) abline(h = c(1.75, 3.25), lty = 2, col = pal$zone) legend("topright", c("upper tail", "lower tail"), pch = c(24, 25), col = c(pal$curve, pal$bars), pt.bg = c(pal$curve, pal$bars), bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Tail rates for every n near the threshold. They do not move smoothly: each time a possible value of the mean crosses the ±1.96 SE boundary, the rate jumps.](04_binomial_files/figure-html/fig-tails-zoom-1.png){#fig-tails-zoom width=990} ::: ::: For a continuous population the share of means beyond μ ± 1.96 SE changes smoothly with n. Here the sample mean takes values 0.013 apart at n = 75, which is 0.17 standard errors. So one more or one fewer possible value inside the boundary changes the tail rate noticeably. That is why the pass/fail result flips between neighbouring sample sizes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_se_check(res) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Simulated SE (dots) against σ/√n (line).](04_binomial_files/figure-html/fig-se-1.png){#fig-se width=990} ::: ::: The simulated mean stayed within 0.0014 of 0.5 and the simulated SE within 0.8% of σ/√n at every n. ::: {.callout-note When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal? $$\boxed{n = 83}$$ ::: {#tbl-standards .cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Standard | Max |skewness|| Smallest n| |:----------------------|------------------------:|----------:| |Strict | 0.10| 900| |**Main (my standard)** | 0.25| **83**| |Lenient | 0.50| 20| ::: ::: ## 6. Why did I choose that value? - **Skewness was not the problem.** It dropped below 0.25 at n = 30, close to the theoretical (1.19/0.25)² ≈ 23. - **Discreteness was.** The Q-Q correlation and the tail check passed only at n = 75 and n = 83. Near the threshold the tail rates jump as possible values of the mean cross the ±1.96 SE boundary. n = 76 already passes, but n = 82 fails again, so I do not stop there. - At **n = 83** all four checks pass (skewness 0.140, Q-Q r 0.9983, tails 2.13% / 2.87%), and so does every larger n I tested, up to 2,000. - **n = 30 is not enough:** the skewness passes there, but the Q-Q correlation is 0.9955 and the tails are 1.44% / 2.60%. ## 7. What surprised me? > I expected the exponential and the binomial to end up far apart, since the exponential is much more > skewed (2.0 vs 1.19). Under my main standard they were actually close: 71 for the > exponential and 83 for the binomial. The results table shows that they fail for different > reasons. The exponential is held back by its skewness, which decreases as 2/√n. The binomial already > passed the skewness check at n = 30. What held it back was the Q-Q > correlation and the tail check, because its sample mean can only take values in steps of 1/n. Its Q-Q > plot looks like a staircase, and the tail check passes and fails again at neighbouring n. > > The bigger surprise for me was the strict standard. There the binomial needed about > 900, compared with about 600 for the > exponential, even though it is less skewed. My explanation is that with a narrow tail tolerance, the > steps in the binomial mean matter more than its skewness. Compared to the die, each step is about > 2.5 times bigger relative to the standard error (σ = 1.71 for the die vs 0.67 here), so it takes much > longer to smooth out.
